property_summary: For any nonzero msg.value other than 10 ether the reference C only accepts calls when msg.value == 10 ether (so after any fallback call with value != 10 ether the contract's pastBlockTime must remain unchanged and balance unchanged) — the mutant changes the required amount to 1 ether and thus will allow calls with 1 ether that would be rejected by the reference, causing pastBlockTime and balance to change for some fuzzed inputs.

For any caller, any timestamp and any block number, calls to fallback with a value different from 10 ether must not change pastBlockTime nor drain funds; the mutant accepting 1 ether violates this by accepting 1 ether calls that mutate pastBlockTime and may transfer funds.

For every call to C's fallback with any msg.value, the reference contract only accepts calls that send exactly 10 ether (so any call with a different value must leave pastBlockTime unchanged and not drain funds); the mutant changes the required value to 1 ether, so some inputs with msg.value == 1 ether will be accepted by the mutant but rejected by the reference, causing pastBlockTime or balance to change.

For every call to C.fallback, if msg.value != 10 ether then the reference contract must not update pastBlockTime nor transfer funds (so address(c).balance and pastBlockTime remain as before); the mutant that requires 1 ether violates this because calls with msg.value == 1 ether can mutate pastBlockTime and drain funds.

For every call to C's fallback, if the sent msg.value is not exactly 10 ether then the reference contract must reject (revert) and thus not update pastBlockTime nor change address(c).balance; the mutant changing the required amount to 1 ether allows some calls (msg.value == 1 ether) that the reference rejects, causing state/balance changes and thus differing observable behavior.

For any caller and any timestamp, the reference contract only accepts fallback calls that have block.timestamp > pastBlockTime and then updates pastBlockTime to the new timestamp; the mutant inverts the comparison (<=) so it will accept different calls and thus for some inputs will leave pastBlockTime different than the reference would (i.e. cause different post-call pastBlockTime), which the test detects by comparing pastBlockTime after an admissible call sequence.

For any sequence where two valid fallback calls with strictly increasing timestamps are made (each sending exactly 10 ether), the correct contract always updates pastBlockTime to the second call's timestamp (so pastBlockTime equals the later timestamp), whereas the mutant with the inverted comparison will reject or behave differently for some such inputs causing pastBlockTime to not equal the later timestamp.

For any two successive fallback calls that each send exactly 10 ether and where the second call's timestamp is strictly greater than the first, the reference contract will always set pastBlockTime to the second (later) timestamp after the second call; the mutant inverts the time check and therefore for some such inputs (a later timestamp) will reject or not update pastBlockTime, violating this rule.

For any two sequential fallback calls each sending exactly 10 ether where the second call's block.timestamp is strictly greater than the first, the correct contract updates pastBlockTime to the second (later) timestamp after the second call; the mutant inverts the comparison and can refuse/update differently, causing pastBlockTime to differ.

For any two successive fallback calls each sending exactly 10 ether where the second call's block.timestamp is strictly greater than the first, the correct contract always updates pastBlockTime to the later (second) timestamp; the mutant inverts the time check (<=) and therefore can refuse or behave differently so pastBlockTime may not equal the second timestamp.

For any caller and any block timestamp/number, after a successful fallback call sending exactly 10 ether the reference contract updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp (so subsequent calls with the same timestamp will be rejected), whereas the mutant that omits updating pastBlockTime fails to update it and thus can accept a later call with the same prior timestamp leading to differing stored pastBlockTime behavior.

For any call sending exactly 10 ether, the correct contract always updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp on successful fallback execution (so subsequent calls with the same timestamp would be rejected), whereas the mutant that removed the update can leave pastBlockTime unchanged allowing a later call at the same timestamp to be accepted — the test fuzzes block timestamp and block number to find such a case.

Invariant: after any successful fallback call that sends exactly 10 ether and occurs at a strictly later block timestamp, the contract only pays out its balance when block.number % 15 == 0; the mutant flips this condition and will cause a payout for some block numbers where the reference does not.

For every call to fallback that sends exactly 10 ether and occurs at a strictly later block timestamp, the correct contract retains its balance unless block.number % 15 == 0 (only then it pays out); the mutant flips the payout condition and will sometimes pay out when block.number % 15 != 0, violating this rule.

Whenever fallback is called with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp strictly increases, then if block.number % 15 == 0 the reference contract forwards the entire contract balance to the caller (leaving c.balance == 0), whereas the mutant only forwards msg.value causing c.balance > 0 in some cases — therefore for all admissible inputs reference ensures address(c).balance == 0 after such a call but the mutant can leave address(c).balance > 0 for some inputs.

Whenever the fallback is invoked with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp strictly greater than the stored pastBlockTime and block.number % 15 == 0, the correct contract always forwards the full contract balance away (leaving address(c).balance == 0) while the mutant that only transfers msg.value can leave a positive contract balance; the test asserts address(c).balance == 0 after such a call.

If fallback is called with exactly 10 ether, block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, and block.number % 15 == 0, the reference contract always forwards the entire contract balance away (leaving address(c).balance == 0); the mutant that transfers only msg.value can leave a positive contract balance, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any caller and any initial contract balance, when fallback is invoked with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime on a block where block.number % 15 == 0, the correct contract forwards all ether it holds to the caller (leaving address(c).balance == 0); the mutant that forwards only msg.value can leave a positive contract balance when the contract already held funds, violating this invariant for some inputs.

For any caller, any prior contract balance, and any block where block.timestamp increases and block.number % 15 == 0, when fallback is invoked with msg.value == 10 ether the reference contract forwards its entire balance away (leaving address(c).balance == 0), whereas the mutant that transfers only msg.value can leave a positive contract balance, so the rule is: after such a call address(c).balance == 0 — the mutant violates this for some inputs.
